name: Iodine
summary: Iodine is a mineral the thyroid gland needs to make thyroid hormones, which set the body's energy use and guide growth and brain development before birth and in childhood. Both too little and too much can upset the thyroid.
roles: Building block of the thyroid hormones (T4 and T3)
Brain and body development of the unborn baby and young child

status.note: There is no routine test of one person's iodine status. Iodine in urine is used to judge groups: EFSA treats a median urinary iodine of 100 µg/L or more in school-age children as a sign that a population gets enough. One person's urine iodine changes a lot from day to day; one study found about 10 repeated samples were needed for a reliable individual estimate. TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) and free T4 (free thyroxine), which this app tracks, show how the thyroid is working, not how much iodine someone eats: they are often normal with mildly low intake and can be abnormal for many other reasons.

signs: Signs of an underactive thyroid: tiredness, feeling cold, weight gain, dry skin, constipation
In pregnancy, a risk to the baby's brain development; severe deficiency can cause serious developmental problems in the child
atRisk: Pregnant and breastfeeding women, who need more
People who eat little or no dairy, fish or eggs, such as vegans, unless they use iodised salt or fortified foods
People who use non-iodised salts (many sea salts and rock salts)
People living where soil is low in iodine and salt is not iodised

signs: With very large single amounts: burning mouth and throat, stomach pain, nausea, diarrhoea
high.note: Too much iodine can make the thyroid either underactive or overactive, especially in people with an existing thyroid condition, with nodules in the thyroid, or who lived for a long time with low iodine intake. Seaweed and kelp products are the most common cause of very high intakes, because their iodine content varies widely and can be extremely high. Some medicines (amiodarone) and iodine-containing contrast dyes also deliver large amounts.

examples: White fish and seafood, such as cod and haddock
Milk, yoghurt and cheese (in many European countries)
Seaweed, with very variable and sometimes extremely high amounts
foodSources.note: The iodine in milk and in plants depends on animal feed and soil, so amounts differ between countries and seasons. Most plant drinks contain little iodine unless the label says they are fortified.

forms.name: Potassium iodide and potassium iodate
forms.note: The forms used in most supplements, multivitamins, prenatal supplements and iodised salt. They give a known, steady amount.

forms.name: Iodised salt
forms.note: The main way countries prevent iodine deficiency. The amount added differs by country. Using iodised salt is about the type of salt, not about eating more salt.

forms.name: Kelp and other seaweed supplements
forms.note: Seaweeds differ greatly in iodine, and some, such as kombu (kelp), can give far more than the upper limit. The EU Scientific Committee on Food warned that iodine-rich seaweed products, especially dried ones, can give dangerously high intakes. Seaweed can also contain arsenic, cadmium and lead.

forms.name: Iodine drops and Lugol's solution
forms.note: Concentrated solutions that can give very large amounts in a few drops.

forms.name: Potassium iodide tablets for radiation emergencies
forms.note: High-dose tablets that block the thyroid from taking up radioactive iodine. They are meant only for a nuclear emergency, when the authorities say so, not as a supplement.

upperLimit.note: For iodine from all sources, in adults, including pregnancy and breastfeeding. Set by the EU Scientific Committee on Food (2002) and still listed in EFSA's overview of upper limits (August 2025). It comes from small changes in TSH, without illness, at about 1,700–1,800 µg a day, divided by 3 for safety. It does not apply to people from areas with long-standing iodine deficiency, who are more sensitive, or to treatment with iodine under medical supervision.

interactions.note: Needs are higher, and many prenatal supplements already contain iodine. Seaweed and kelp products are risky because their iodine content is unpredictable. Ask a midwife or doctor before adding iodine.

interactions.with: Thyroid conditions (Hashimoto's, Graves' disease, thyroid nodules or goitre)
interactions.note: Extra iodine can trigger an overactive or underactive thyroid, especially with nodules or thyroid antibodies. Talk to your doctor before using iodine or seaweed supplements.
Iodine changes how the thyroid works, which can affect the treatment. Large amounts can interfere with medicines for an overactive thyroid.
Contains a lot of iodine and can itself cause thyroid problems, so extra iodine needs a doctor's view.
Lithium can cause an underactive thyroid, and large amounts of iodine may add to that effect.

interactions.with: Iodine contrast dye and iodine antiseptics
interactions.note: X-ray and CT contrast dyes and iodine skin antiseptics can deliver large amounts of iodine. Mention recent scans with contrast when thyroid tests are done.

cautions: Kelp and other seaweed products vary widely in iodine and can give far more than the upper limit.
With a thyroid condition, talk to your doctor before using iodine supplements.
TSH and free T4 are thyroid tests, not iodine tests.
Iodised salt is a way to get iodine, not a reason to eat more salt.

commonUses: May support normal thyroid function and steady energy, because the thyroid needs iodine to make its hormones.
May support a baby's brain development in pregnancy, since thyroid hormones guide growth of the developing brain.
May help the body's metabolism, the way it turns food into energy, through thyroid hormones.

origin: Iodine is a mineral found in seawater and soil. Foods take it up from the sea or the soil, so it is high in sea fish, shellfish and seaweed, and is also found in dairy and eggs. Many countries add it to table salt to prevent deficiency.
Supplement iodine is usually potassium iodide or potassium iodate, made industrially. Kelp and other seaweed supplements are dried sea plants, and their iodine content varies widely.
dosage: The European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) sets an adequate intake (AI) of 150 µg a day for adults, 200 µg in pregnancy and 200 µg when breastfeeding. For iodine from all sources the upper limit (the most that is likely safe every day) is 600 µg a day for adults, set by the EU Scientific Committee on Food and still listed by EFSA. It does not apply to people from areas of long-standing iodine deficiency, who are more sensitive, or to treatment under medical supervision. These are population values, not personal targets.

An amount commonly used in studies and supplements is about 150 to 200 µg a day. A trial in mildly deficient children used 150 µg a day, and a trial in pregnant women in India and Thailand used 200 µg a day. This is not a reference intake or a personal recommendation.

On a label, check the form (potassium iodide or iodate) and the amount in µg per serving. Kelp and other seaweed products vary greatly and some can give far more than the upper limit, and iodine drops or Lugol's solution can give very large amounts in a few drops. Many prenatal supplements already contain iodine. Extra iodine can trigger an overactive or underactive thyroid, especially with thyroid nodules, Hashimoto's disease, Graves' disease or thyroid medicines, and it can interact with amiodarone and lithium. Anyone with a thyroid condition, or who is pregnant, should ask a doctor or midwife first. Iodised salt is a way to get iodine, not a reason to eat more salt.

targets.label: Amount commonly used in studies and supplements

foodAmounts.verdict: Partly. White fish and shellfish are rich in iodine, and dairy and eggs add useful amounts, so people who eat them regularly can reach the reference intake. People who eat little fish or dairy may fall short, and the iodine in food depends on the soil, feed and country, so iodised salt or a supplement matters more for them. Seaweed varies so widely that it can give far too much. For example, for the EFSA adequate intake, adults, about 40 g of haddock, grilled, or about 60 g of mussels, cooked; for the amount commonly used in studies and supplements, about 50 g of haddock, grilled, or about 80 g of mussels, cooked.
foodAmounts.notChecked: Food values are from the UK food composition table (McCance and Widdowson's CoFID 2021) built into this app, for the food named. Cooked, stored or processed foods and other brands differ. These are amounts eaten, not absorbed.
